title: Compare the major architecture styles: Monolith, Modular Monolith, Microservices, Layered (N-Tier), Microkernel/Plugin, Hexagonal (Ports & Adapters), Space-Based, Peer-to-Peer: and the problem each one actually solves.
shortTitle: Compare the major architecture styles: Monolith, Modular Monolith, Microservices, Layered, Microkernel, Hexagonal, Space-Based, Peer-to-Peer: and the problem each one solves.
keyPoints: Monolith: one deployable unit solving simplicity; right default for small teams.
Modular Monolith: one deployable with enforced module boundaries solving maintainability without distribution.
Microservices: independently deployable services solving team autonomy and independent scaling at the cost of distributed complexity.
Layered (N-Tier): horizontal layers solving separation of concerns; applied inside a monolith or a service.
Microkernel/Plugin: stable core plus plugins solving extensibility (product engines, IDEs).
Hexagonal (Ports and Adapters): domain in the center with technology-agnostic ports solving testability and technology independence.
These styles are not mutually exclusive; a real bank platform combines several on different axes.

s1_definition.oneliner: Every architecture style exists to solve one dominant problem -- pick the style whose problem matches yours, because choosing the wrong one buys complexity you do not need.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Monolith** – one deployable unit; solves simplicity.
- **Modular Monolith** – one deployable with enforced module boundaries; solves maintainability without distribution.
- **Microservices** – independently deployable services; solves independent scaling and team autonomy at the cost of distributed complexity.
- **Layered (N-Tier)** – horizontal layers (controller, service, repository); solves separation of concerns.
- **Microkernel/Plugin** – stable core plus plugins; solves extensibility.
- **Hexagonal (Ports and Adapters)** – domain in the center with technology-agnostic ports; solves testability and technology independence.
- **Space-Based** – in-memory data grid; solves extreme bursty load by removing the database bottleneck.
- **Peer-to-Peer** – no central coordinator; solves decentralization (blockchain, mesh).
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India as a building. A Monolith is one big open-plan office. A Modular Monolith is the same building with walled departments. Microservices are separate buildings across the city. Layered is one building with floors. Microkernel is a core with pluggable product modules. Hexagonal is a department designed so it does not care whether customers arrive by phone, web, or in person. Space-Based is a trading floor keeping everything in fast memory. Peer-to-Peer is a network of branches that gossip directly with no head office.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Architecture styles each solve one dominant problem, and the skill is matching the style to the problem. A monolith solves simplicity and is the right default for a small team. A modular monolith keeps that simplicity but enforces internal boundaries, and is the recommended starting point. Microservices solve independent deployment and team autonomy, but cost distributed complexity that only pays off with multiple teams needing independence.

The code-organization styles -- layered, microkernel, hexagonal -- live inside a deployable, not instead of one. A real banking platform combines several: microservices for deployment, hexagonal inside each service for testability, a microkernel product engine, and a space-based hot trading path.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj started with a modular monolith, extracted only the fraud service when it needed independent scaling, and applied hexagonal architecture inside each service. The classic mistake is reaching for microservices because they look impressive when a modular monolith solves the actual problem with far less pain.

Remember one sentence: every architecture style exists to solve one specific problem, so pick the style whose problem matches yours and combine styles across deployment and code-organization dimensions.
